key_insight: This paper tackles multi-modal classification when any subset of modalities may be missing at training or test time, not just the common two-modality case. It introduces a co-learning perspective so models can still learn useful shared representations and remain effective under arbitrary modality dropouts.
problem_solved: Real-world multi-modal systems often face missing inputs due to sensor failures, privacy constraints, cost limits, or deployment mismatches between training and inference. Existing approaches mostly target bimodal settings or rely on fusion methods that are not designed for arbitrary missing modality patterns.
method: Adopts a multi-modal co-learning framework instead of focusing only on robust late/early fusion.
Learns from incomplete modality combinations so the model can generalize to arbitrary missingness at inference time.
Targets classification scenarios where the available modality set can vary across samples, rather than assuming a fixed input structure.
impact: This is important for practitioners building real-world AI systems that must operate reliably with incomplete data. It can improve robustness, reduce dependence on every sensor being present, and make multi-modal models easier to deploy in messy, practical environments.
visual_elements: A modality grid showing all possible combinations of present/missing inputs.
A pipeline diagram comparing standard fusion methods vs. co-learning.
An icon set for sensors, privacy, and failures illustrating why modalities go missing.
A performance chart showing accuracy under increasing modality missingness.
paper_title: Co-Learning for Missing Arbitrary Modalities in Multi-modal Classification
paper_authors: Francisco Mena, Dino Ienco, Roberto Interdonato, Cassio F. Dantas, Simon Besnard
